Apple today accused a new UK proposal targeting App Store fees of amounting to price controls, warning it could harm innovation and investment. Here are the details.

Apple hits back at UK App Store regulation

According to Reuters, Apple today filed a formal response to a consultation from the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment options.

The CMA gained the power to impose such requirements after designating Apple and Google as having "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets last year. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, that designation gives regulators the power to introduce company-specific rules designed to boost competition and give consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still charge a commission on transactions that go through alternative payment methods, but any such fees would have to be considered "fair and reasonable."

Reuters notes that the CMA "expects the redirected fees to be lower than current app store charges, with the savings passed on to UK consumers or reinvested into developers' businesses to support innovation."

Apple, however, disagrees, and has pushed back on the proposal. Here's the Reuters report:

The CMA rejected Apple's characterization of the proposal as price controls, saying it is setting out principles for judging whether redirected fees are fair and reasonable, rather than dictating fee levels.
